title: CI/CD & Serving for ML: Gates, Canaries & Model Servers
summary: How a registered model safely reaches users: an automated validation gate that checks overall, per-slice and latency criteria, a canary release that exposes a small, stable share of traffic and decides from enough evidence, and a model server that validates inputs and batches requests without mixing up answers.
takeaways: A validation gate compares the candidate with production, not just with a fixed bar. It checks the metric floor, the allowed regression, every important slice, and a latency percentile.
A better overall metric can hide a broken slice, so check slices separately.
Canary routing must hash request ids with a stable function (sha256, crc32), never Python's per-process hash(), so assignment is sticky across replicas and ramps.
Don't call a canary on a handful of requests. Wait for a minimum sample, then compare error rates. A server can batch for throughput, but each answer must go back to the request that asked.

steps.label: Candidate
steps.detail: A new version is registered with its offline metrics, per-slice metrics and benchmark latencies.

steps.label: Validation gate
steps.detail: CI compares it with production: metric floor, max regression, every slice, p95 latency. Any failure blocks the release.

steps.label: Canary
steps.detail: Deploy beside production. A stable hash of the request id sends a small percentage of traffic to the candidate.

steps.label: Canary analysis
steps.detail: Once both arms have enough requests, compare error rates and promote, roll back, or keep collecting.

steps.label: Ramp & serve
steps.detail: Raise the percentage step by step (sticky users stay put) until the candidate serves everyone.

terms.definition: An automated check in the release pipeline that blocks a model unless it meets agreed criteria relative to production.
A meaningful subset of the evaluation data (device, country, customer tier) whose metric is checked separately.
Rolling a new version out to a small subset of traffic first, watching it, then ramping up or rolling back.
The same user or request id always lands in the same arm, and raising the canary percentage only adds users to it.
The value at rank ceil(q·n/100) in the sorted sample. It is always an observed value.
Grouping concurrent requests into one model call to raise throughput, then splitting the outputs back to their callers.
